proposedTopics.title: Storage gas
proposedTopics.description: Storage is the EVM's most expensive resource, so most gas wins come from touching it less: pack variables, prefer warm access, cache reads, and avoid writes. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity

proposedTopics.title: Calldata & memory gas
proposedTopics.description: The two transient data locations have their own costs: calldata is read-only and cheap, memory is priced per word plus a quadratic expansion term. Choosing and sizing them well cuts intrinsic and runtime gas. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/

proposedTopics.title: Control-flow gas
proposedTopics.description: Loops and conditionals run many times, so small per-iteration savings compound: order short-circuits, drop overflow checks where safe, cache lengths, and return early. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity

proposedTopics.title: Types & layout gas
proposedTopics.description: The EVM is a 256-bit machine, so type and data-structure choices have non-obvious gas effects: smaller types can cost more, bitmaps beat arrays of bools, and mappings beat arrays for keyed access. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity

proposedTopics.title: Assembly & Yul gas
proposedTopics.description: Dropping to inline assembly skips the safety scaffolding solc emits — memory allocation, return-data copies, bounds checks — for hand-tuned gas, at the cost of losing those guarantees. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/

proposedTopics.title: Architecture-level gas
proposedTopics.description: The biggest wins are structural: deploy clones instead of full contracts, share a singleton, batch calls, push work off-chain, and let users pull instead of looping to pay them. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity

proposedTopics.title: Packing variables into slots
proposedTopics.description: The compiler lays out state variables sequentially and packs consecutive fields smaller than 32 bytes into one 32-byte slot. Fields packed together can be read or written with a single SLOAD/SSTORE, turning several storage ops into one; declaring them in the wrong order wastes a whole slot. Cold SSTORE of a fresh slot is 20000 gas, so eliminating one slot is a large win. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/internals/layout_in_storage.html
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/SlotPacking.sol — reorder a struct/state layout so a hot getter reads one slot; beat 23000 gas on the two-write path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the write path under 23000 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Warm vs cold access (EIP-2929)
proposedTopics.description: EIP-2929 made the first access to a storage slot or account address in a transaction 'cold' and cheaper 'warm' afterward: cold SLOAD is 2100 gas, warm SLOAD 100; the first touch of an external account is 2600 vs 100 warm. An EIP-2930 access list can pre-warm slots/addresses to move that cost into the intrinsic phase. Repeated access to the same slot pays warm price, so grouping accesses helps. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2929
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/WarmCold.sol — restructure so a repeated storage/account read is warm rather than cold; beat the cold baseline by ~2000 gas. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the second access at ~100 not ~2100 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Minimizing SLOAD and SSTORE
proposedTopics.description: Storage ops dominate gas: a warm SLOAD is 100, a cold one 2100, an update SSTORE 2900 warm / 5000 cold, and a fresh 0→nonzero SSTORE 20000. Collapsing redundant reads and writes — accumulate in a local and write once — is the single highest-leverage micro-optimization. Writing the same value back still charges, so guard no-op writes. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/StorageWrites.sol — an accumulator loop that currently SSTOREs each iteration; rewrite to write once after the loop; beat 30000 gas for a 10-iteration accumulate-then-write. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows one SSTORE and total gas under 30000.

proposedTopics.title: Caching storage in memory
proposedTopics.description: Reading a stack/memory local costs about 3 gas, while re-reading storage costs 100 (warm) or 2100 (cold). Loading a storage variable once into a local and reusing it — instead of reading the state variable repeatedly in a loop or expression — saves ~97 gas per avoided warm read. Struct fields and array elements benefit most. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/CacheStorage.sol — a function that reads a state variable N times in a loop; hoist it into a local; beat 3000 gas for a 20-iteration read loop. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows only one SLOAD for that variable and total gas under 3000.

proposedTopics.title: constant vs immutable for gas
proposedTopics.description: Both avoid the ~2100 cold SLOAD entirely. A `constant` is inlined into the bytecode at every use site at compile time; an `immutable` is assigned once in the constructor and baked into the deployed code, then read as a cheap push rather than from storage. Use `constant` for compile-time-known values and `immutable` for values fixed at deploy (e.g. an owner or token address). Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/contracts.html#constant-and-immutable-state-variables
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Immutable.sol — convert a storage config value that never changes after deploy into an immutable; beat 500 gas on the read path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the read path with no SLOAD for that value, under 500 gas.

proposedTopics.title: SSTORE refunds (EIP-3529)
proposedTopics.description: Clearing a storage slot to zero earns a gas refund of 4800, which incentivizes freeing state. EIP-3529 (London) cut the refund cap from 50% to 20% of the transaction's total gas used and removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund, so refunds can no longer make a tx nearly free. Design patterns that clear-then-set within one tx rarely pay off after 3529. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3529
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Refunds.sol — a function that deletes stale slots; measure net gas after the 20%-of-used refund cap; beat 3000 gas net per cleared slot. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the refunded net cost under 3000 gas and matches your hand-computed value.

proposedTopics.title: Transient storage for gas (EIP-1153)
proposedTopics.description: TSTORE and TLOAD (Cancun, EIP-1153) read/write a transaction-scoped storage that auto-clears at the end of the tx, each costing ~100 gas with no 20000-gas set and no refund accounting. This makes it ideal for reentrancy locks and transient accounting (e.g. Uniswap V4 flash accounting) that previously paid an SSTORE-set then an SSTORE-clear. It is not persistent, so never use it for durable state. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1153
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/TransientLock.sol — replace an SSTORE-based reentrancy guard with a TSTORE/TLOAD lock. Done when: forge test passes (guard still blocks reentry) and forge snapshot shows the lock cost ~100 not ~20000+refund gas.

proposedTopics.title: Packing structs and enums
proposedTopics.description: A struct follows the same slot-packing rules as top-level state: ordering members so small ones (uint8, bool, address's 20 bytes, uint96) share a 32-byte slot cuts the slots read/written together. Enums are stored as uint8, so several fit in a slot with other small fields. A poorly ordered struct silently spends an extra 20000-gas slot per stored item. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/internals/layout_in_storage.html
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/StructPacking.sol — reorder a 4-field struct (e.g. address + uint96 + uint64 + bool) so it fits in two slots instead of four; beat 45000 gas on the full store path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the store path under 45000 gas (two fewer fresh-slot SSTOREs).

proposedTopics.title: calldata over memory
proposedTopics.description: For external functions, declaring reference-type arguments (arrays, bytes, structs) as `calldata` instead of `memory` avoids copying the data into memory (a CALLDATACOPY of 3 gas/word plus memory-expansion cost) — you read fields directly from calldata. The copy is pure waste when the function only reads the argument. `memory` is only required if the function mutates the argument locally. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/types.html#data-location
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/CalldataArgs.sol — change a read-only `bytes memory`/`uint[] memory` external param to calldata and drop the copy; beat 2000 gas on a 4-word argument. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the call under 2000 gas, the eliminated CALLDATACOPY.

proposedTopics.title: Custom errors over require strings
proposedTopics.description: A `require(cond, "msg")` stores the revert string in bytecode and ABI-encodes it on revert; a custom `error Foo(); ... revert Foo();` compiles to just a 4-byte selector (plus any typed args). This shrinks deployment bytecode and saves roughly 50 gas on each revert path, while carrying structured data. Since Solidity 0.8.26 `require(cond, CustomError())` is also supported. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/contracts.html#errors-and-the-revert-statement
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/CustomErrors.sol — replace require-string reverts with custom errors; beat 300 gas on the revert path. Done when: forge test passes (reverts with the right selector) and forge snapshot shows lower deploy size and the revert path under 300 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Shrinking calldata
proposedTopics.description: Every calldata byte is charged before execution: 16 gas per nonzero byte and 4 per zero byte (EIP-2028). Tighter encoding — smaller integer types, fewer padded 32-byte words, packing several small args, or custom compact encodings decoded on-chain — lowers this intrinsic cost, which matters a lot on L2s where calldata/blob data dominates fees. Zeros are cheap, so left-padding is nearly free but the value bytes are not. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2028
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/ShrinkCalldata.sol — replace an over-wide argument set with a packed encoding decoded on-chain; beat 2500 gas total including intrinsic calldata cost. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows total gas (including intrinsic) under 2500.

proposedTopics.title: Avoiding memory expansion
proposedTopics.description: Memory is priced at 3 gas per 32-byte word plus a quadratic term (words² / 512), so cost grows faster than linearly as the highest touched offset increases. Allocating large or sparse buffers, or repeatedly growing memory in a loop, gets expensive fast; reuse a buffer and size it once. The quadratic term is negligible for small buffers but dominates past a few KB. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/MemoryExpansion.sol — a function that grows memory each loop iteration; preallocate/reuse one buffer instead; beat 50000 gas for a 20-iteration buffer-write loop. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the quadratic expansion cost removed and total gas under 50000.

proposedTopics.title: abi.encodePacked encoding cost
proposedTopics.description: `abi.encodePacked` drops the 32-byte padding that `abi.encode` applies, producing fewer bytes to hash, store, or copy — cheaper when you hash a fixed set of fixed-width values. The catch: packing two or more dynamic types (string/bytes) can produce ambiguous concatenations that collide under keccak256, so use `abi.encode` (or fixed-width fields) when hashing multiple dynamic args. Choose packed only when the layout is unambiguous. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/abi-spec.html#non-standard-packed-mode
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/EncodePacked.sol — hash a set of fixed-width fields with encodePacked instead of encode, keeping it collision-safe; beat 200 gas on the encode+hash path. Done when: forge test passes (hash matches expected) and forge snapshot shows the encode path under 200 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Short-circuit ordering
proposedTopics.description: `&&` stops evaluating at the first false operand and `||` at the first true one. Ordering operands so the cheapest and most-decisive condition runs first — e.g. a calldata or memory comparison before a 2100-gas cold SLOAD, or a common-case check before a rare one — avoids paying for the expensive operand when the cheap one already decides. This is free to apply and never changes semantics for side-effect-free conditions. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/ShortCircuit.sol — reorder a compound require so the cheap check gates the expensive storage read; beat 500 gas on the common-reject path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the common-reject path under 500 gas, never paying the SLOAD.

proposedTopics.title: Unchecked increments
proposedTopics.description: Solidity 0.8+ inserts overflow/underflow checks on every arithmetic operation (an extra comparison and a conditional revert branch). Wrapping a provably-safe operation — most commonly a loop counter that cannot overflow the loop bound — in `unchecked { ++i; }` removes that check and saves roughly 30–40 gas per iteration. Only do this where you can prove no wrap occurs. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/UncheckedLoop.sol — sum a fixed 256-element array with the loop-counter increment moved into an unchecked block; beat 120000 gas. Done when: forge test passes with a correct sum and forge snapshot shows the function under 120000 gas.

proposedTopics.title: ++i over i++
proposedTopics.description: `i++` evaluates to the pre-increment value, so the compiler keeps a temporary copy of the old value; `++i` returns the new value and needs no copy. When the returned value is unused — as in a loop counter — `++i` (ideally `unchecked{++i}`) is a few gas cheaper per iteration. The difference is small individually but compounds across long loops. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/PreIncrement.sol — switch a loop counter from i++ to ++i (inside unchecked); beat 5 gas per iteration, under 500 gas total for a 100-iteration loop. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows total gas under 500 with unchanged output.

proposedTopics.title: Caching array length
proposedTopics.description: Writing `for (uint i; i < arr.length; ++i)` re-reads `arr.length` every iteration. For a storage array that is an SLOAD each time (2100 cold, then 100 warm); for a memory array it is a cheaper MLOAD but still avoidable. Caching the length in a local before the loop turns N reads into one. This is a classic, safe, high-frequency win in any iteration-heavy contract. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/CacheLength.sol — hoist a storage array's length out of the loop condition; beat 3000 gas for a 20-iteration loop over a storage array. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows one length read instead of one per iteration, total gas under 3000.

proposedTopics.title: Removing redundant checks
proposedTopics.description: Checks that can never fail, or that duplicate a guarantee already enforced, are pure gas cost: re-validating an input a modifier already checked, a zero-address check on a value the type or a prior call already constrains, or SafeMath on top of 0.8's built-in checks. Removing genuinely dead checks (never the load-bearing ones) trims each call. The skill is proving a check is truly redundant before deleting it. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/RedundantChecks.sol — remove a check the compiler or a prior guard already guarantees, without weakening safety; beat 200 gas per call. Done when: forge test passes (including the negative cases) and forge snapshot shows gas under 200 for the call path with the check removed.

proposedTopics.title: Early return
proposedTopics.description: Returning as soon as the result is known avoids executing the rest of the function — skipping later storage reads, loops, or computation on the common path. Structuring a function to handle cheap/frequent cases first and return, rather than computing everything then selecting, lowers average gas. It also tends to make the control flow clearer. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/EarlyReturn.sol — restructure a function to return on the trivial case before the expensive branch; beat 500 gas on the trivial-case path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the trivial-case path under 500 gas, skipping the costly work.

proposedTopics.title: Word-size choices
proposedTopics.description: The EVM operates on 256-bit words, so a standalone `uint8` or `uint128` is not cheaper than `uint256` — the compiler emits extra masking to keep the narrow value in range, making it slightly more expensive for a variable that isn't packed with others. Use `uint256` by default for standalone variables and loop counters, and reach for narrow types only when several pack into one storage slot. Getting this backwards is a common false optimization. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/WordSize.sol — compare a standalone uint8 counter vs uint256 and pick the cheaper; beat 1000 gas for a 20-iteration counting loop. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot confirms the uint256 path is under 1000 gas, cheaper than uint8 for the unpacked case.

proposedTopics.title: bytes32 over string
proposedTopics.description: A short identifier stored as `bytes32` fits a single 32-byte word with no length field and none of the dynamic-array machinery, whereas `string`/`bytes` store a length and, if longer than 31 bytes, spill data into separately-hashed slots. For fixed-size labels, keys, or symbols up to 32 bytes, `bytes32` is markedly cheaper to store, read, and compare. Only use `string` when the value is genuinely variable-length or user-facing. Resources: 🔗 https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/internals/layout_in_storage.html
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Bytes32Label.sol — store a fixed short label as bytes32 instead of string; beat 25000 gas on the store path. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the store/read path under 25000 gas, avoiding the dynamic-string cost.

proposedTopics.title: Bitmaps for boolean flags
proposedTopics.description: Storing many boolean flags as individual bools or mapping entries burns one slot each (a 20000-gas set apiece on first write). Packing up to 256 flags as bits of a single `uint256` and setting/testing them with bit masks means one SSTORE covers a whole batch — the technique behind gas-efficient merkle-airdrop claim tracking. Trades a little masking arithmetic for enormous storage savings. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Bitmap.sol — replace a mapping(uint=>bool) claim tracker with a uint256-word bitmap keyed by index; beat 25000 gas per claim call. Done when: forge test passes (claims still one-shot) and forge snapshot shows one SSTORE per 256 flags, per-claim gas under 25000.

proposedTopics.title: Mappings vs arrays
proposedTopics.description: A `mapping` does keyed lookup by hashing the key to a slot — no bounds checks and no length bookkeeping — so it is cheaper for random read/write. A dynamic array maintains a length slot (an extra SSTORE on push) and bounds-checks indexing, and is only necessary when you must enumerate or preserve order. Default to a mapping for keyed access and add an array only when iteration is truly required. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/MappingVsArray.sol — replace a linear-scan array lookup with a mapping keyed by id; beat 3000 gas for a lookup over a 50-element dataset. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the O(1) keyed access under 3000 gas, beating the array scan.

proposedTopics.title: Cheap hashing in assembly
proposedTopics.description: keccak256 costs 30 gas plus 6 per word hashed, but the Solidity `keccak256(abi.encode(a, b))` form also allocates and copies memory. Writing the two 32-byte inputs to the scratch space (0x00–0x40) and calling `keccak256(0x00, 0x40)` in assembly skips the abi.encode allocation — the standard trick for computing a mapping's storage slot cheaply. You must keep inputs within scratch space and not clobber the free-memory pointer. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmHash.sol — compute keccak256 of two words via scratch-space assembly instead of abi.encode; beat 100 gas on the encode+hash path. Done when: forge test passes (hash equals the abi.encode result) and forge snapshot shows the path under 100 gas, the memory allocation removed.

proposedTopics.title: Direct storage slots in assembly
proposedTopics.description: Reading or writing a fixed storage slot with `sload`/`sstore` in assembly bypasses Solidity's automatic layout, letting you use deterministic slots for reentrancy guards, ERC-7201 namespaced storage, or diamond storage. It also avoids some of the compiler's defensive code. The danger is a wrong slot silently corrupting unrelated state, so slots are usually derived from a keccak of a namespace string. Resources: 🔗 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7201
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmSlot.sol — store a guard flag at a fixed keccak-derived slot via sstore/sload; beat 5000 gas on the guard-check-and-set path. Done when: forge test passes (guard works, no collision with other state) and forge snapshot shows the assembly path under 5000 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Low-level calls in Yul
proposedTopics.description: Using `call`/`staticcall`/`delegatecall` in Yul lets you control forwarded gas, skip the return-data copy Solidity performs automatically, and avoid the implicit extcodesize check on high-level external calls. This trims gas on hot call paths (e.g. token transfers, multicall dispatch) but you must handle the success boolean and returndata manually or risk silently ignoring a failed call. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmCall.sol — perform an external call in assembly, handling success and returndata yourself, cheaper than the high-level call; beat 200 gas on the call-overhead path. Done when: forge test passes (reverts propagate correctly) and forge snapshot shows the call overhead under 200 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Bit masking
proposedTopics.description: Bitwise AND with a mask extracts or cleans bytes far more cheaply than higher-level slicing: `and(x, 0xff...ff)` isolates a packed field, clears dirty high bits (e.g. after an address cast), or reads one lane out of a packed slot. Shifts (`shl`/`shr`) position the field first. This is how packed structs and bitmaps are read/written efficiently in assembly. Getting the mask width wrong reads neighboring bits, so masks must match the field size exactly. Resources: 🔗 https://www.evm.codes/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Masking.sol — read and update one packed field of a slot with shift+mask instead of struct accessors; beat 3000 gas on the read-modify-write path. Done when: forge test passes (neighboring fields untouched) and forge snapshot shows the masked path under 3000 gas.

proposedTopics.title: Function selector optimization
proposedTopics.description: Solidity's dispatcher compares the incoming 4-byte selector against each external function's selector to route the call. Because the compiler orders selectors and (in linear dispatch) checks them in order, naming functions so that frequently-called ones get small, low-value selectors that are compared first saves a few gas on every call to them. Tools mine function-name suffixes to produce leading-zero selectors; the win is per-call and adds up on hot entrypoints. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Selector.sol — rename a hot function (via a suffix) so its selector sorts ahead of colder ones in the dispatcher; beat 50 gas on dispatch overhead for the hot call. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the hot call's dispatch overhead under 50 gas, fewer selector comparisons.

proposedTopics.title: Minimal-proxy clones for gas (EIP-1167)
proposedTopics.description: EIP-1167 deploys many identical contracts as tiny 45-byte proxies that `delegatecall` to one shared implementation. Deploying a clone costs a few thousand gas versus the full contract's deployment (which pays 200 gas per code byte), an order-of-magnitude saving for factories minting many instances. The trade-off is a delegatecall on every call and the need to initialize via a function rather than a constructor. Resources: 🔗 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1167
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Clones.sol — deploy instances via an EIP-1167 clone factory (OpenZeppelin Clones) instead of `new`; beat 60000 gas per instance deploy. Done when: forge test passes (clone behaves like the implementation) and forge snapshot shows deploy gas under 60000, an order of magnitude lower than a full `new` deploy.

proposedTopics.title: Singleton contracts
proposedTopics.description: Instead of deploying a contract per instance, a singleton holds all instances' state and logic behind one address — Uniswap V4's PoolManager for every pool, ERC-4337's EntryPoint for every wallet. This eliminates repeated deployment cost and enables cross-instance optimizations like flash accounting in transient storage. The cost is a more complex access model, since one contract now mediates all instances. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Singleton.sol — refactor a per-instance contract into a singleton keyed by an id, sharing one deployment; beat 5000 gas for registering a new instance. Done when: forge test passes (instances isolated by key) and forge snapshot shows registering a new instance under 5000 gas, no per-instance deploy cost.

proposedTopics.title: Batching and multicall
proposedTopics.description: Every transaction pays a 21000-gas base cost and cold-access charges up front. Aggregating many operations into one transaction — a `multicall` that loops over encoded calls, or a batch function — amortizes that base cost and lets later operations reuse warm storage slots and warm accounts. Users save both the repeated 21000 and repeated cold-to-warm transitions. Watch that batched calls don't let one failure silently skip the rest. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/Multicall.sol — add a batch entrypoint that executes N encoded ops in one tx, reusing warm state; beat 84000 gas for a 5-op batch (vs 5 separate txs' base cost). Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot shows the 5-op batch under 84000 gas, cheaper than 5 separate txs.

proposedTopics.title: Pull over push payments
proposedTopics.description: Looping to push funds to N recipients pays a transfer (and cold-account cost) per recipient and reverts entirely if one recipient's receive reverts — a gas and denial-of-service liability. The pull pattern instead credits each recipient's balance (one SSTORE) and lets them withdraw themselves, moving the gas to the claimer and removing the loop and the griefing vector. It is both a gas and a security optimization. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/PullPayments.sol — convert a push-in-a-loop distribution into credit-then-withdraw; beat 30000 gas for crediting 5 recipients. Done when: forge test passes (one reverting recipient can't block others) and forge snapshot shows crediting 5 recipients under 30000 gas, free of the per-recipient transfer loop.

proposedTopics.title: Off-chain compute, on-chain verify
proposedTopics.description: Do the expensive work off-chain and have the contract only verify a succinct proof of the result. A merkle airdrop verifies an ~log(n)-hash proof instead of storing every eligible claim on-chain; a signed message (EIP-712) authorizes an action without maintaining on-chain permission state; a ZK proof attests to a computation the chain never runs. Verification is cheap; storage and re-computation are not. The trade is added off-chain infrastructure and data-availability assumptions. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/gas-optimization-in-solidity
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/MerkleClaim.sol — gate an airdrop on a merkle proof verified on-chain instead of a stored eligibility mapping; beat 50000 gas for a single claim verify+mark-claimed. Done when: forge test passes (valid proof claims, invalid reverts) and forge snapshot shows a claim under 50000 gas, far below storing all claims individually.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does declaration order of small state variables affect gas, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Consecutive fields <32 bytes pack into one 32-byte slot, so fields used together share one SLOAD/SSTORE; a fresh slot's first write is 20000 gas. Pitfall: interleaving a full-word field between small ones breaks packing and wastes a whole slot.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a two-field storage layout (a uint128 and a uint128) that the compiler packs into one slot.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint128 a; uint128 b; // declared consecutively → both live in slot 0. Reading/writing both together costs one SLOAD/SSTORE.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve the storage-packing gas puzzle in the RareSkills gas-puzzles repo.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Reorder fields so hot ones pack into a single slot; measure with forge snapshot until under target.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Under EIP-2929, what do cold and warm access cost for a storage slot and for an account?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Slot: cold SLOAD 2100, warm 100. Account: cold 2600, warm 100. First touch in a tx is cold. Pitfall: an EIP-2930 access list pre-warms but you pay that cost up front in the intrinsic phase.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a snippet that reads the same storage variable twice so only the first read pays cold cost.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 x = s; // cold 2100 ... uint256 y = s; // warm 100 — better: cache in a local `uint256 v = s;` and reuse v (≈3 gas).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve a warm/cold access gas puzzle from the RareSkills gas-puzzles repo.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Reorder or dedupe accesses so repeat touches are warm (100) not cold (2100/2600); snapshot under target.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Rank warm SLOAD, cold SLOAD, update SSTORE, and fresh 0→nonzero SSTORE by cost.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: warm SLOAD 100 < cold SLOAD 2100 < warm-update SSTORE 2900 (cold-update 5000) < fresh 0→nonzero SSTORE 20000 is the priciest. Pitfall: writing the same value back still charges — guard no-op writes.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a loop that accumulates into a local and writes storage once at the end.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 sum; for (uint256 i; i < n; ++i) { sum += a[i]; } total = sum; // one SSTORE instead of one per iteration.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is caching a storage variable in a local worth it even for warm reads?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A stack/memory local read is ~3 gas vs 100 for a warm SLOAD (2100 cold), so each avoided re-read saves ~97 gas. Pitfall: if the value can change mid-function (e.g. via an external call) the cache can go stale.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a loop condition and body that read a state variable `count` only once.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 c = count; for (uint256 i; i < c; ++i) { ... } // read `count` into c once, use c throughout.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do `constant` and `immutable` each avoid an SLOAD, and when do you use which?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: constant is inlined into bytecode at compile time; immutable is set in the constructor and baked into the deployed code, read as a push. Use constant for compile-time values, immutable for deploy-time ones. Pitfall: immutable can only be assigned in the constructor.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an immutable owner set at deploy and a constant fee.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address public immutable owner; uint256 public constant FEE = 100; constructor() { owner = msg.sender; } // neither read costs an SLOAD.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does clearing a slot refund, and what did EIP-3529 change?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Clearing nonzero→zero refunds 4800 gas. EIP-3529 (London) capped refunds at 20% of gas used (down from 50%) and removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund. Pitfall: you can't make a tx nearly free by clearing state anymore.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a function that frees a slot to earn a refund.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: delete balances[user]; // or balances[user] = 0; sets nonzero→zero, queuing a 4800 refund (subject to the 20%-of-used cap).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is a TSTORE/TLOAD reentrancy lock cheaper than an SSTORE-based one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: TSTORE/TLOAD cost ~100 gas each and auto-clear at tx end, avoiding the SSTORE-set (20000) then SSTORE-clear (with capped refund) an SSTORE lock pays. Pitfall: transient storage is wiped at tx end — never use it for state that must persist.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a reentrancy guard using transient storage (tstore/tload).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { if tload(0) { revert(0,0) } tstore(0,1) } _; assembly { tstore(0,0) } // ~100 gas per op, auto-clears at tx end.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you order struct members to minimize slots, and where do enums fit?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Place fields so small ones (uint8/bool/uint96 + a 20-byte address) sum to ≤32 bytes per slot; enums store as uint8 and pack alongside. Pitfall: a mis-ordered struct silently spends an extra 20000-gas slot per stored item.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a struct that packs an address, a uint96, and a bool into two slots.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: struct P { address owner; uint96 amount; bool active; } // owner(20)+amount(12)=32 → slot 0; active → slot 1.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is a read-only external array argument cheaper as calldata than memory?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: memory copies the argument in (CALLDATACOPY 3 gas/word + memory expansion); calldata is read in place. Pitfall: you can't mutate a calldata argument — use memory only if you must modify it locally.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an external function signature that reads a bytes argument without copying it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function f(bytes calldata data) external { ... } // `calldata` avoids the memory copy a `bytes memory` param would force.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do custom errors save gas versus require strings?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A custom error is a 4-byte selector (plus typed args) instead of a stored, ABI-encoded string — smaller deploy bytecode and ~50 gas less per revert. Pitfall: off-chain tooling must decode the selector to show a human message.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Rewrite `require(x > 0, "zero")` using a custom error.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: error Zero(); ... if (x == 0) revert Zero(); // or (solc ≥0.8.26) require(x > 0, Zero());

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the intrinsic gas costs of calldata bytes, and how do you lower them?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 16 gas per nonzero byte, 4 per zero byte (EIP-2028). Use narrower types, fewer padded words, and packed/custom encodings decoded on-chain. Pitfall: matters most on L2s where calldata/blob data dominates fees.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a call that packs two uint8 args into one bytes32 instead of two padded words.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 packed = bytes32(uint256(a) << 8 | uint256(b)); // one 32-byte word decoded on-chain vs two padded args.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How is memory priced, and why does a large buffer get expensive fast?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 3 gas per 32-byte word plus a quadratic term (words²/512), charged to the highest offset touched. Pitfall: growing memory inside a loop repeatedly pays expansion — preallocate/reuse one buffer.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a loop that reuses one preallocated memory buffer instead of allocating each iteration.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes memory buf = new bytes(32); for (uint256 i; i < n; ++i) { /* overwrite buf */ } // allocate once, reuse.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is abi.encodePacked cheaper than abi.encode, and when is it unsafe?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Packed drops 32-byte padding → fewer bytes to hash/copy, cheaper for fixed-width fields. Pitfall: concatenating two+ dynamic types (string/bytes) can collide under keccak256 — use abi.encode or fixed-width there.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a collision-safe keccak256 over two fixed-width values using encodePacked.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint256(a), address(b))); // fixed-width operands → unambiguous, cheaper than abi.encode.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does operand order in `&&`/`||` save gas?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: && stops at the first false, || at the first true, so put the cheapest/most-decisive operand first (e.g. a calldata compare before a cold SLOAD). Pitfall: only reorder side-effect-free operands, or you change behavior.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Reorder `require(store[id].active && msg.sender == admin)` to gate the SLOAD.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: require(msg.sender == admin && store[id].active); // cheap calldata/immutable compare first; the SLOAD only runs if it passes.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does `unchecked { ++i; }` save gas, and when is it safe?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 0.8+ adds an overflow check (compare + revert branch) on every arithmetic op; unchecked removes it, saving ~30–40 gas/iteration. Safe when the counter provably can't overflow (bounded by the loop). Pitfall: unchecked anywhere a wrap is possible reintroduces overflow bugs.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a for-loop whose counter increment is unchecked.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: for (uint256 i; i < n;) { /* body */ unchecked { ++i; } } // i < n < 2^256, so the increment can't overflow.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is `++i` cheaper than `i++` when the return value is unused?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: i++ returns the pre-increment value, so the compiler keeps a temporary copy; ++i returns the new value and skips the copy — a few gas per iteration. Pitfall: the difference only exists when you don't use the expression's value.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the cheapest loop-counter increment idiom for an unused return value.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: unchecked { ++i; } // pre-increment, no temporary copy, and no overflow check.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why cache `arr.length` before a loop over a storage array?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The condition re-reads length each iteration — an SLOAD (2100 cold, then 100 warm) for a storage array; caching in a local makes it one read. Pitfall: don't cache if the loop body changes the array's length.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a loop over a storage array `items` that reads its length only once.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 len = items.length; for (uint256 i; i < len;) { ... unchecked { ++i; } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes a check safe to remove, and give an example of a redundant one.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Remove only checks whose condition is already guaranteed — e.g. SafeMath on top of 0.8's built-in overflow checks, or re-validating an input a modifier already checked. Pitfall: deleting a load-bearing check to save gas is how exploits get introduced — prove redundancy first.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Rewrite `unchecked`-safe addition that drops a redundant SafeMath-style check under solc 0.8.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 c = a + b; // 0.8 already reverts on overflow — no need for a manual `require(c >= a)`.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does returning early lower average gas?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Returning as soon as the result is known skips the remaining storage reads/loops/computation on the common path. Pitfall: ensure the early path still runs any required state updates before returning.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a function that returns immediately when the amount is zero, before any storage work.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function f(uint256 amt) external { if (amt == 0) return; /* expensive storage work only for amt > 0 */ }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can a standalone `uint8` cost more gas than a `uint256`?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The EVM works on 256-bit words, so a narrow unpacked type needs extra masking to stay in range, making it costlier. Pitfall: use uint256 for standalone vars/loop counters; narrow types only pay off when several pack into one slot.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the cheaper type choice for a standalone counter and say why.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 i; // not uint8 — no masking overhead for an unpacked, full-word variable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is a short fixed label cheaper as bytes32 than as string?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 fits one word with no length field and no dynamic-array machinery; string stores a length and (if >31 bytes) spills into hashed slots. Pitfall: bytes32 caps you at 32 bytes — use string for genuinely variable-length data.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a mapping from a bytes32 key to a value instead of a string key.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(bytes32 => uint256) public byKey; // bytes32 key is one word — cheaper to store/compare than a string key.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a bitmap beat 256 individual bool slots, and what's the cost?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 256 flags become bits of one uint256 slot, so one SSTORE covers a batch instead of a 20000-gas set per flag. Cost: extra shift/mask arithmetic to read/write a bit. Pitfall: index arithmetic bugs corrupt neighboring flags.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write set-bit and test-bit for a uint256 bitmap `bits` at index i (i < 256).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bits |= (1 << i);  // set   bool isSet = (bits >> i) & 1 == 1; // test

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is a mapping cheaper than an array, and when do you still need an array?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Mapping: no bounds checks, no length slot → cheaper keyed read/write. Array: needed to enumerate/preserve order, and push pays an extra length SSTORE. Pitfall: mappings aren't iterable — track keys separately if you must enumerate.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a keyed record store using a mapping instead of a scanned array.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(uint256 => Record) public records; // O(1) records[id] lookup vs an O(n) array scan.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you compute a mapping slot's keccak256 cheaply in assembly?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Write key and slot to scratch space (0x00 and 0x20) and call keccak256(0x00, 0x40) — skips abi.encode's memory allocation; keccak is 30 + 6/word. Pitfall: don't overflow past 0x40 into the free-memory area or you corrupt it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that hashes two 32-byte words via scratch space.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x00, a) mstore(0x20, b) let h := keccak256(0x00, 0x40) }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why use sload/sstore on a fixed slot, and how do you avoid collisions?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Fixed-slot assembly bypasses Solidity's layout for guards, ERC-7201, or diamond storage, avoiding some defensive code. Derive the slot from keccak of a namespace string (minus one) to avoid clashing with declared state. Pitfall: a wrong/overlapping slot silently corrupts unrelated storage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly to read and write a value at a fixed namespaced slot.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 constant SLOT = keccak256("my.namespace"); assembly { let v := sload(SLOT) sstore(SLOT, add(v, 1)) }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does calling in Yul save, and what must you handle yourself?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It skips Solidity's automatic return-data copy and implicit extcodesize check and lets you control forwarded gas. You must check the success flag and handle returndata (returndatacopy) manually. Pitfall: ignoring the success bool silently swallows a failed call.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a Yul call that reverts if the callee fails.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { let ok := call(gas(), target, 0, add(data,0x20), mload(data), 0, 0) if iszero(ok) { returndatacopy(0,0,returndatasize()) revert(0, returndatasize()) } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you read one packed field out of a slot with shift and mask?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Shift the field down (shr) then AND with a mask sized exactly to the field (e.g. 0xff for 8 bits). Pitfall: a mask wider than the field reads neighboring bits — match the mask to the field width exactly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly to extract the low byte of a word `x`.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { let b := and(x, 0xff) } // isolates bits 0–7; use shr first to read a higher field.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How can function naming reduce dispatch gas?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The dispatcher compares the 4-byte selector against each function's; giving hot functions small, low-value selectors (via a mined name suffix) that sort/compare first saves a few gas per call. Pitfall: with --via-ir the dispatcher can binary-search, shrinking the benefit — measure before mining.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Show how a mined name suffix changes a function's selector.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes4 sel = bytes4(keccak256("transfer_hot(address,uint256)")); // a chosen suffix yields a smaller selector that dispatches earlier.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is deploying an EIP-1167 clone so much cheaper than a full contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A clone is a 45-byte proxy that delegatecalls one shared implementation, so you pay a few thousand gas instead of the full deploy (200 gas/byte of code). Pitfall: no constructor — you must initialize the clone via a function, and guard re-initialization.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a clone-factory deploy using OpenZeppelin Clones.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address c = Clones.clone(implementation); IInit(c).initialize(args); // ~few-thousand-gas deploy vs `new Impl()`.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a singleton architecture cut gas versus a contract per instance?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: One deployed contract holds all instances keyed by id (Uniswap V4 PoolManager, ERC-4337 EntryPoint), removing per-instance deploy cost and enabling shared optimizations like transient flash accounting. Pitfall: one contract mediating all instances concentrates risk and complicates access control.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a singleton state layout keyed by an instance id.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(bytes32 => Pool) internal pools; // one contract, per-id state, no per-instance deployment.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What costs does batching many operations into one tx amortize?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The 21000-gas per-tx base cost and cold-access charges — later ops in the batch reuse warm slots/accounts (100 vs 2100/2600). Pitfall: a batch must decide whether one failing sub-call reverts all or is skipped — silent skips hide failures.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a multicall that executes an array of encoded self-calls.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function multicall(bytes[] calldata calls) external { for (uint256 i; i < calls.length;) { (bool ok,) = address(this).delegatecall(calls[i]); require(ok); unchecked { ++i; } } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is pull-payment both cheaper and safer than pushing in a loop?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pushing pays a transfer (+cold account) per recipient and reverts entirely if one recipient reverts; pull credits a balance (one SSTORE) and lets each withdraw, moving gas to the claimer and removing the DoS. Pitfall: still guard the withdraw against reentrancy (CEI).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write credit-then-withdraw functions replacing a push loop.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function credit(address u, uint256 a) internal { owed[u] += a; } function withdraw() external { uint256 a = owed[msg.sender]; owed[msg.sender] = 0; payable(msg.sender).transfer(a); }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a merkle airdrop save gas over storing every claim on-chain?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Store only a 32-byte root; each claimant submits an ~log(n)-hash proof the contract verifies, instead of an SSTORE-set per eligible address at setup. Pitfall: still track claimed status (a bitmap) so a valid proof can't be replayed.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the on-chain verify step for a merkle-proof-gated claim.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 leaf = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, amount)); require(MerkleProof.verify(proof, root, leaf)); // then mark claimed in a bitmap.
